html:
The walled palace city of the Nguyễn dynasty in Huế, central Vietnam, begun in 1804 under the first Nguyễn emperor, Gia Long, and enlarged to its full size by 1833.

Gia Long, of the old Nguyễn lords family, had defeated the Tây Sơn and united the whole country in 1802, the first time one ruler held it from north to south. He made Huế, his family's old seat, the capital. Inside a great citadel on the Perfume River, the Imperial City held halls of state, temples to the ancestors, gardens and offices. At its heart was the Purple Forbidden City, for the emperor and his household. The plan followed Chinese ideas and was modelled in part on Beijing's Forbidden City, with some European style ramparts.

Huế stayed the capital under French rule in French Indochina, until the last emperor, Bảo Đại, gave up the throne here in 1945. The city was badly damaged in 1968 during the Battle of Huế in the Vietnam War. UNESCO listed the monuments of Huế in 1993.
